text: Published October 18, 2026 KOLKATA, INDIA: A stampede at a Hindu religious festival in the eastern Indian city of Kolkata killed 17 people and injured 25 others on Saturday, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said, as Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced compensation for the victims' families.

The incident occurred at around 7:40 pm local time at the exit gate of the Sarada Park, also known as the Chorbagan, Durga Puja pandal in the city's Girish Park area, according to a statement by Kolkata Police.
Police attributed the incident to heavy crowds of festival visitors amid rainfall.

The injured were rescued and taken to Medical College and Hospital for treatment, the police statement said, adding that police reinforcements, firefighters, disaster management personnel, ambulances and medical teams had been deployed.
The pandal was closed to visitors following the incident, police said.
Adhikari said 17 people had been brought dead to hospital and 25 others were injured.
He visited the hospital where the injured were being treated, according to reports by Press Trust of India.
Modi expressed sorrow over the deaths and extended condolences to the bereaved families, the Prime Minister's Office said in a statement published by the government's Press Information Bureau.

The government announced compensation of 200,000 rupees ($2,106) from the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund for the next of kin of each person killed, while those injured would receive 50,000 rupees each, the statement said.
The government also said the West Bengal administration was providing assistance to affected families.

Durga Puja is one of the largest annual religious and cultural festivals in West Bengal, drawing large crowds to temporary structures known as pandals, where idols of the Hindu goddess Durga are displayed for worship.
The festival celebrates the goddess's victory over the demon Mahishasura and is marked by elaborate decorations, religious ceremonies and public gatherings across the state.
The cause of the crowd surge was not independently established in the official information available.
Reports carried by Indian media cited differing accounts of how the incident unfolded, including the impact of rainfall and a rush among people near the venue's entrance and exit.

Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN - By Reuters - - Oct 19, 2026 CNN chief international anchor Christiane Amanpour will leave next year, after 43 years with the network, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters on Monday.
The news channel has recently come under the ownership of Skydance, whose CEO David Ellison has faced criticism over his stewardship of CBS News.
Christiane Amanpour will end her daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year.
She will continue to host a weekly program on CNN through May and work on a transition through June.

Amanpour, whose first major assignment was covering the first Gulf War, went on to report from conflicts in Bosnia, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran over a career spanning more than three decades.
The announcement comes as Skydance, formerly Paramount Skydance, completed its $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros.
Discovery earlier this month, bringing CNN and CBS News under the same corporate roof.
CNN chief Mark Thompson and CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss will keep their roles, with both reporting to David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz.
The deal has drawn scrutiny on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have criticized Ellison for allegedly tailoring news coverage at CBS News to favor President Donald Trump.
Christiane Amanpour is a British-Iranian journalist and one of the most recognizable international correspondents of the past 30 years.
She first gained prominence at CNN covering the first Gulf War in 1990 from Baghdad, and went on to report from major conflict zones including Bosnia, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Iraq, Ukraine and Iran.

Known for her on-the-ground reporting and tough interviews with world leaders, she became CNN’s Chief International Anchor and hosted Amanpour, the network’s flagship global affairs interview program.
She also anchored a weekly edition of the show on PBS, making her a rare dual presence on both cable and public television in the U.S.
Her career has been defined by a focus on war, diplomacy, and human rights, with a reporting style that blends eyewitness coverage with in-depth interviews.

Over the decades she has interviewed presidents, prime ministers, and activists across five continents, and has won multiple awards including several News & Documentary Emmys and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the International Women’s Media Foundation.
In late 2025 it was announced she would step down from her daily CNN and PBS shows at year’s end, while continuing a weekly CNN program into 2026.

Railways' modernisation to play key role in boosting economy: PM Premier opens new Shalimar Express along with upgraded waiting areas, CIP lounges in Karachi Cantt Station Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Monday that digitising and modernising Pakistan Railways, along with upgrading passenger facilities, would significantly boost the national economy.
He said the federal government, in collaboration with the Sindh government, would modernise the Karachi Circular Railway (KCR) and upgrade all railway stations across the province and the country.
The prime minister expressed these views while addressing the inauguration ceremony of the new Shalimar Express and the newly upgraded waiting rooms and CIP lounges at Karachi Cantt Railway Station.

Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah, Federal Minister for Railways Muhammad Hanif Abbasi, Federal Minister for Information and Broadcasting Attaullah Tarar, and other dignitaries were present on the occasion.
The prime minister said that soon after assuming office, Abbasi worked diligently to modernise the railway system.
After revamping Lahore Railway Station, Karachi Cantt Station has also been upgraded with contemporary facilities.
He said that all railway stations in the province would be modernised in coordination with the Sindh government to ensure better travel facilities for the passengers.

He said like Sindh and Punjab, such coordination with the governments of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan should be evolved, which would ultimate make the Pakistan Railways the best transport system of this region.

PM Shehbaz said the railways freight system is also being organised, while the federal and Sindh governments have a partnership to provide transportation for Thar coal, with both governments investing 50% each in the project.
He assured that all required funds would be released in this regard so that the set targets of the projects could be achieved.
The premier said the Shalimar Express running between Karachi and Lahore has been converted into a new, upgraded train.
He described Karachi as not only the economic hub but also "the heart of Pakistan".
He reiterated that cooperation with the provincial governments of Punjab, Sindh, KP, and Balochistan would continue to ensure modernisation across the railway network and help stabilise the economy.
The prime minister praised Abbasi's leadership, calling him the "hero of today’s ceremony", and congratulated him for transforming the outdated railway system.
He said the federal government would work with all provinces to extend the railway network to Central Asia, specifically highlighting the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway line project.
He also emphasised reviving the Islamabad–Tehran-Istanbul rail route, which would boost our economy to the heights.

The prime minister noted that Abbasi has initiated discussions with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) for a $2 billion loan to further upgrade Pakistan Railways' line from Karachi to Rohri, and that it would ultimately be connected to the Reko Diq project.
Responding to CM Shah's request to include the KCR project in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the prime minister assured full cooperation, calling it a vital initiative.

China targets solar supply chain with new export restrictions on key technologies China proposes strict export controls on 12 advanced solar technologies to protect its dominant green-energy supply chain China's Ministry of Commerce has proposed a new set of export controls targeting 12 advanced solar-manufacturing technologies and core equipment, citing national security and strategic interests.

The ministry released a statement on Friday that it proposed the photovoltaic technologies to China's export-control list, adding that greater oversight is needed because solar technologies are increasingly being used in sensitive areas like aerospace and national defense.

The sweeping proposal is part of a broader regulatory overhaul spanning 40 key technologies—including artificial intelligence and biopharmaceuticals—designed to protect Beijing’s dominant technological edge in the renewable energy sector as countries like the U.S. and India ramp up domestic manufacturing.
Next-Gen solar cells targeted: The draft splits the targeted solar technologies into two tiers: items facing complete export prohibitions and those requiring strict export licensing/restrictions.
Manufacturing know-how for cutting-edge perovskite and perovskite-silicon tandem cells (which boast high efficiency rates) face strict export bans.

The restrictions cover advanced production methods for ultra-thin silicon wafers (70 µm or less), large-scale fluidized-bed polysilicon manufacturing processes, and high-efficiency cell tech like TOPCon and xBC variants.

Because China controls a vast majority of the global solar supply chain, the proposed measures threaten to complicate international expansion plans, raise capital expenditure costs for western clean energy projects, and shift equipment supply dynamics.
The draft is currently open for public consultation through mid-November, with interim pre-export registration measures enacted in the interim.

Trump-Xi summit: China sees ‘surprise’ surge in U.S. orders China saw surprise jump in US orders ahead of Trump-Xi summit A private survey found a surprising increase in how American businesses ramped up orders from Chinese manufacturers leading up to the high-stakes summit this week as companies are poised for sustained stability between the world’s two largest economies.
Primarily, the estimate measuring orders from the US calculated as the proportion of surveyed firms reporting an increase minus in the share reporting a decrease jumped to 13 in September.
Meanwhile, overall Chinese domestic and export orders remain depressed compared to their levels a year earlier.

The upsurge in US-bound orders came as businesses were positioned for a more cooperative accord between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping who is in Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade.
The two countries agreed to a two-month extension through January that keeps tariffs lower, eases restrictive controls on rare earth exports and holds off higher port fees on ships.

The export order figures are consistent with recent metrics including that China’s ports saw their busiest week on record in the lead up to the summit, and are another sign that trade flows were recovering amid hopes for a further easing in bilateral tensions.

Washington is inclined to fast-tracked expedited Chinese approval of rare-earth licenses for US end users as well as higher consumer spending on US agricultural goods, Beijing meanwhile would expect the White House to uphold the existing halt on defense transactions to Taiwan.

The two leaders are expected to meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November, potentially at the risk of being sidelined from the G20 summit the US is hosting in Miami in December, though no bilateral meeting after this week’s summit has yet been confirmed.

The province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the third-largest province of Pakistan by population and the smallest province by area, is divided into 40 districts and seven divisions.
History 1901 to 2010 Districts have formed an integral part of civil administration in the subcontinent since colonial times.

When the North-West Frontier Province (the former name of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) formed in November 1901, it was divided into five "settled districts": Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan, Hazara, Kohat, and Peshawar, and a "trans-border tract" of land which encompassed five "Political Agencies": Khyber, Kurram, Malakand, Tochi, and Wano.
The four districts Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan, Kohat, and Peshawar were considered "Trans-Indus" districts.

By the time of the 1941 census of British India, Tochi Agency had been renamed "North Waziristan Agency", Wana Agency had been renamed "South Waziristan Agency", and two tehsils of Peshawar District (Mardan and Swabi) were split off to form Mardan District, which became the fifth "Trans-Indus" district.

The six districts of the North-West Frontier Province had also all been given their own "Frontier Regions", which were tribal areas that were under the control of the deputy commissioner of an adjacent district.

1947 to 1954 Upon the independence of Pakistan, the six districts of the North-West Frontier Province retained their borders and status within the province, but the five tribal agencies and six frontier regions all split off from the province, creating the Federally Administered Tribal Areas.
The Federally Administered Tribal Areas was an administrative unit of Pakistan governed from Islamabad which had an area larger than the province itself.
In 1951, parts of Malakand Agency were split off to create the Mohmand Agency in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas.
1954 to 1972 In 1954, the One Unit policy that consolidated all of West Pakistan into one province began.
From 1954 to 1970, the North-West Frontier Province ceased to exist.
The death of the province brought the rise of the area's first divisions (divisions had already existed in Punjab and East Bengal, but none of the other provinces had any divisions until One Unit).
The area that once covered the North-West Frontier Province and Federally Administered Tribal Areas was split among two divisions: Dera Ismail Khan Division and Peshawar Division.

Dera Ismail Khan Division covered Bannu District, Dera Ismail Khan District, North Waziristan Agency, and South Waziristan Agency, and Peshawar Division covered Hazara District, Kohat District, Mardan District, Peshawar District, Kurram Agency, Khyber Agency, Malakand Agency, and Mohmand Agency.
The frontier regions which had previously existed were absorbed into their respective districts at this time.

The One Unit policy ended in 1970 and the provinces returned with their original forms (which also meant that the Federally Administered Tribal Areas and the North-West Frontier Province were separate once more, and that the Frontier Regions regained their status as administrative units).
The divisions that had been created as a result of the policy stayed in the North-West Frontier Province, but were abolished entirely in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas.

This meant that at the North-West Frontier Province was divided into three divisions and ten districts, while the Federally Administered Tribal Areas were divided into six Political Agencies and four Frontier Regions.
The agency of Orakzai was created out of parts of the Frontier Region Kohat (which still existed, but was smaller) in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas.

This meant that by the time of the 1981 Census of Pakistan, the North-West Frontier Province had 12 districts (two more than in 1972) organized into four divisions (one more than in 1972) and the Federally Administered Tribal Areas had seven Political Agencies (one more than in 1972) and four Frontier Regions.

As for the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, the agencies remained the same and retained the exact same borders they had in 1981, but two more frontier regions were created: Frontier Region Lakki Marwat and Frontier Region Tank.
These two frontier regions were created from parts of Frontier Region Dera Ismail Khan, which was, in 1981, split up into two non-contiguous sections.

The northern section was divided into Frontier Region Lakki Marwat and Frontier Region Tank upon the creation of Lakki Marwat and Tank Districts, but Frontier Region Dera Ismail Khan retained the southern section.

This meant that by the time of the 1998 Census of Pakistan, the North-West Frontier Province had 24 districts (twelve more than in 1981) organized into seven divisions (three more than in 1981) and the Federally Administered Tribal Areas had seven Political Agencies and six Frontier Regions (two more than in 1981).

You can find a list of them below (districts and divisions which do not exist anymore are in italic): 1998 to 2017 In August 2000, all of the divisions throughout Pakistan were abolished, but were reinstated in their exact previous forms eight years later after the elections of 2008.
On the other hand, no changes occurred to the 1998 district setup for over a decade, until 2010, when the North-West Frontier Province was renamed Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One year later, in 2011, Kala Dhaka Tehsil was separated from Mansehra District to become Torghar District, the 25th district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
These 25 districts (the 24 districts dating to 1998 and Torghar) were the only districts recorded as a part of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during the 2017 Census.

This meant that by the time of the 2017 Census of Pakistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had 25 districts (one more than in 1998) organized into seven divisions and the Federally Administered Tribal Areas had seven Political Agencies and six Frontier Regions.

You can find a list of them below (districts and divisions which do not exist anymore are in italic): 2017 to present In 2014, Kohistan District was bifurcated into Upper Kohistan District and Lower Kohistan District, but tensions on the bifurcation did not resolve until late 2017 (after the 2017 census), when Kolai-Palas District was formed as well.

This meant that Kohistan District was still legally one administrative unit until after the time of the 2017 census (the bifurcation was delayed in light of the political tensions, and did not go through until late 2017, when Kohistan district was split into three districts).
On 31 May 2018, the Twenty-fifth Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan was put into force.
This amendment merged the Federally Administered Tribal Areas with the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and changes the province's borders and layout drastically.
The six Frontier Regions joined the districts they were adjacent to (Frontier Region Bannu was incorporated into Bannu District, Frontier Region Kohat was incorporated into Kohat District etc.).
In late 2018, Chitral District, formerly the largest district in the province by area, was bifurcated into Upper Chitral District, from Mastuj Tehsil, and Lower Chitral District, from Chitral Tehsil.
In 2022, South Waziristan district was bifurcated into Upper South Waziristan headquarter Spinkai Karzai and Lower South Waziristan headquarter Wana.
In January 2023, Alai was given full district status from the tehsil of Battagram.
In January 2023, Allai was elevated to full district status from the Allai Tehsil of Battagram.
In October 2025, the KP government divided the Swat district into Upper Swat District and at the same time created Paharpur District from part of Dera Ismail Khan.

Published October 18, 2026 Fresh clashes broke out in Paris on Sunday a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with protests over high prices leaving one demonstrator dead, thousands arrested and shops across the country looted or damaged.
One protester died after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in Paris.
Police made more than 2,000 arrests across France, while more than 600 officers were injured, the interior minister said.

"It's like a war zone here," said Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who had come to Paris with his children to visit a friend and said the protests forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique, a trouble hotspot on Saturday.
Police again fired tear gas towards protesters at Place de la Republique and bikes were set on fire on Sunday afternoon, a sign that tensions had not fully subsided in the capital.

More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long student movement with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services.
President Emmanuel Macron will address the nation at 8 p.m. local time (1800 GMT) on Sunday, his office said.
Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt.
The government has blamed the violence on hard-left and ultra-left groups, as well as criminals who it said instigated the looting.
French far-right leader Jordan Bardella said France had been "humiliated" and called on Macron to step down.

"What we are paying for is decades of laxity, a loss of authority, and the moral, psychological, and material disarmament of our internal security forces," he said as he was visiting a police station in Paris.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.

A massive clean-up operation began in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said several hundred shops had been damaged on Saturday.

In Limoges, southwestern France, Mayor Guillaume Guerin denounced the chaos after the city's 143-year-old town hall was set ablaze and largely destroyed in an arson attack on Saturday, drawing comparisons to the 2019 fire that devastated Paris's Notre-Dame Cathedral.
"There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters.

Alberta residents voted to remain part of Canada in the province’s first-ever referendum on separation, in a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the US.
CBC News, Canada’s government-funded national broadcaster, called the result late Monday after 33 per cent of the vote had been counted.
At the time of the call, 76pc of tallied votes were in support of the “remain” side versus 23pc in favour of the province moving forward with a binding vote on separation.

The referendum was nonbinding. “Albertans made a clear choice,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. “They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other.” “Canada is greater than the sum of its parts,” he said.

Pollsters and analysts had repeatedly dismissed the possibility of a separatist victory, citing data that showed about one-third of residents in the western province supported a future referendum on leaving.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the referendum in May, saying it was time to have a vote, understand the will of Albertans on this subject, and move on.
Late Monday, Smith issued a statement on social media saying she was “very pleased” that early results show widespread support for remaining in Canada.

She said she would address Albertans on Tuesday to discuss the results and “where our province goes from here.” A small but vocal group of separatists has campaigned for months for an independent Alberta, arguing that the province’s energy wealth is subsidising poorer parts of Canada and that Alberta would be far richer without Ottawa bureaucracy impeding its path.
Last week, Carney told a rally in Calgary that voting to leave Canada would be a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division, and appealed to Albertans to vote like Canada depends on it.

Carney, who grew up mostly in Alberta, acknowledged that Albertans have often felt slighted by Ottawa and said his government had approved a proposed new pipeline, adding that Alberta is critical to helping Canada reduce its dependence on the US.
Alberta’s referendum follows two previous referendums on separation in the majority French-speaking province of Quebec.
Quebecers voted to stay in Canada in both instances.
First Nations groups have also objected to the idea of an independent Alberta, as their land treaties with Ottawa predate the province’s creation within Canada.
CBC News reported strong turnout from First Nations.

One southern Alberta polling station in an area that is home to the Siksika Nation temporarily ran out of ballots, and then stayed open until after 10 pm MT (9 am PKT) to ensure everyone in line had the chance to vote.
Still, Monday’s referendum is unlikely to end the separatist movement in Alberta.
Before the referendum, some separatist leaders said they would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans voted to remain.
According to data released on October 16 by the pollster Angus Reid, 62pc of Albertans believe there will never be an end to the separatist movement in the province.

Alberta’s referendum also included nine other nonbinding questions on topics including immigration, access to provincial services such as education, social care and healthcare and voter identification requirements.
Results for those questions were still trickling in.

Finance Minister reviews proposed roadmap for gas sector restructuring, deregulation - By Shoaib Nizami - - Oct 19, 2026 Federal Minister for Finance and Revenue, Senator Muhammad Aurangzeb on Monday chaired a high-level meeting to review the proposed restructuring and deregulation roadmap for Pakistan’s gas sector, focusing on financial sustainability, operational efficiency, consumer welfare and greater private-sector participation.

The proposed reforms aim to establish a financially sustainable, efficient and competitive gas market that supports businesses, encourages private investment and protects consumer welfare, said a press release issued by the Ministry of Finance.
The meeting discussed a phased transition towards greater competition, supported by effective regulation, improved operational performance and a more sustainable approach to gas pricing and supply.
Participants reviewed key sectoral challenges, including circular debt, cross-subsidies, unaccounted-for-gas (UFG) losses and supply-demand imbalances.

Discussions focused on addressing legacy liabilities, improving the financial viability of gas utilities and ensuring that existing financial pressures do not undermine the proposed market structure or place an undue burden on consumers.

A sustainable resolution of legacy circular debt and a clear approach to address cross-subsidies were identified as important to the viability of restructured entities and the transition to a competitive market.

The meeting also discussed the expected outcomes of the reform framework, including enhanced energy security, increased private-sector investment, reduced fiscal and sovereign risks, greater business-to-business transactions, more stable and sustainable gas pricing, improved access to competitively priced gas for exporters, and lower system losses through stronger efficiency benchmarks and performance-based incentives.
The Finance Minister emphasized the importance of aligning all stakeholders around a practical and implementable reform architecture.

The proposed framework draws on international experience, including gas-sector reforms in Türkiye and the United Kingdom, while taking into account Pakistan’s institutional structure, market conditions and consumer interests.
Participants also stressed the need for careful sequencing to safeguard security of supply, protect regulated consumers and create a predictable environment for private-sector participation.

The proposed framework will be presented to the Prime Minister, following which further technical work and stakeholder consultations will help refine the reform approach and support an orderly transition.

The meeting reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to advancing gas-sector reforms in a phased and consultative manner to strengthen financial sustainability, improve operational efficiency, attract investment and develop a more competitive gas market while safeguarding consumer interests.

The meeting was attended by the Federal Minister for Petroleum, the Adviser to the Prime Minister on Privatization, the Special Assistant to the Prime Minister on Energy, senior officials from the Petroleum and Finance Divisions, representatives of gas utilities and the World Bank team.

Why Article 140-A must evolve The Punjab Assembly’s recent resolution to amend Article 140-A offers Pakistan a rare constitutional opening to rebuild democracy from the ground up.

The amendment, if expanded to include marginalised sections especially women, religious and ethnic minorities as well as youth to establish a common framework across provinces, could transform how the state connects with its citizens.
Pakistan’s crisis of governance has never stemmed from a lack of laws; it stems from a lack of implementation on the laws.
For nearly eight decades, the state has governed from above, often fearing to empower its citizens at the grassroots.
Every so-called reform in local government has promised devolution, only to end in dissolution.
The result is a cycle of creation and collapse that has denied Pakistanis the one form of governance that directly touches their lives.
When the 18th Amendment introduced Article 140-A in 2010, it was hailed as a turning point.
The new clause made it mandatory for provinces to “establish local governments and devolve political, administrative and financial authority”.
It was supposed to cement the third tier of governance.
Yet fifteen years later, local government remains the weakest link in Pakistan’s democratic chain.
The article itself is skeletal – 41 words that say little about tenure, autonomy or continuity.
It leaves everything to provincial law, and therefore to political whim.
Each province has struggled to sustain continuity in local governance.
In Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan alike, local elections have remained uneven and frequently disrupted.
Poll cycles have been delayed, legal frameworks repeatedly amended and administrative changes introduced midstream.
Even where councils are functioning, elected representatives face persistent issues with limited fiscal space, uncertain tenure and overlapping mandates that dilute their authority.
The pattern is uniform: local democracy exists but is rarely uninterrupted.
That is why the Punjab Assembly’s move this October is so significant.
In a rare moment of unanimity, the assembly adopted a resolution urging the federal government to amend Article 140-A and create a separate constitutional chapter for local governments.
The proposal, forwarded to the National Assembly and Senate, calls for guaranteed autonomy, fixed tenure, and mandatory elections within 90-120 days after dissolution.
It also seeks to prevent premature suspension of local bodies and to anchor their financial and administrative independence.
In substance, this would elevate local governments from creatures of provincial law to constitutionally protected institutions.
It would ensure that devolution is no longer optional but obligatory.

At the federal level, these developments converge with discussions on the 28th Amendment, currently under consideration, which aims to strengthen local governance through clearer constitutional protections, harmonisation of frameworks across provinces, and enforcement of continuity.
If synchronised effectively, this amendment could mark the first coordinated federal-provincial step towards making devolution a constitutional right rather than a political preference.
For Pakistan, local government failure is not new.
Since independence, every political and military regime has tried to shape the system to its own design.

Ayub Khan’s Basic Democracies, Ziaul Haq’s non-party councils, Musharraf’s devolution plan, and the post-2010 provincial frameworks have all claimed to empower citizens but were driven by centralized logic.
Each time, the rhetoric of participation masked the reality of control.
Even today, the structure of local government varies drastically from province to province.
A Union Council in Punjab functions differently from a Town Committee in Sindh or a Village Council in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
These differences may seem administrative, but they weaken the federation.
Without a shared framework or nomenclature, data cannot be compared, responsibilities blur and accountability becomes localized in name but not in effect.
That is why the amendment process must look beyond mere continuity and include forward-looking features chief among them, a minimum common nomenclature for local governments across the country.
Such uniformity would not erase provincial autonomy; it would strengthen coherence.
When a Union Council means the same thing in Lahore, Larkana and Lower Dir, citizens will finally have a common understanding of representation.
It will also enable the Election Commission and other federal bodies to coordinate elections, fiscal planning, and performance monitoring under a shared standard.
Another essential reform is the inclusion of a 33 per cent quota for women at all tiers of local government.
Pakistan’s experience demonstrates that when women are represented in councils, policy priorities shift toward education, health, sanitation, and community welfare.
Yet their participation remains vulnerable to provincial discretion.

A constitutional quota would give permanence to women’s voices in decision-making and align Pakistan with its commitments under CEDAW and the Commonwealth Charter, which recognises gender equality as an essential element of democratic governance.
It would turn representation from a privilege into a right.
Such an amendment would not simply restore local governments; it would redefine Pakistan’s federal compact.
It would transform Article 140-A from a token statement into a living guarantee of democratic participation.
At its heart, this is about more than administrative reform.
It is about reaffirming a democratic philosophy: that governance derives its strength from proximity, not distance.

The Commonwealth Charter captures this truth succinctly when it affirms that “representative local governments and other forms of local governance are essential elements in the exercise of democratic governance”.
If Pakistan truly seeks inclusive, accountable development, it must begin where governance meets daily life in the streets, villages, and neighbourhoods where citizens experience the state.
For too long, Pakistan has spoken the language of devolution while practising centralisation.
The result is visible in weak service delivery, fragile legitimacy and citizens who view government as something external.
The proposed amendment to Article 140-A offers a rare opportunity to change that dynamic.
By embedding continuity, coherence and inclusion into the constitution, Pakistan can finally build a democracy that begins where people live, not merely where power resides.
By constitutionalising local governments, Pakistan can replace political uncertainty with democratic continuity.
That transformation – steady, inclusive and locally anchored – is the reform our federation has long awaited.
The writers are associated with the Sustainable Development Policy Institute (SDPI), Islamabad.

The districts of Pakistan (Urdu: اِضلاعِ پاكِستان) are the third-level administrative divisions of Pakistan, below provinces and divisions, but forming the first-tier of local government.
In total, there are 173 districts in Pakistan. excluding Islamabad Capital Territory.
These districts are further divided into tehsils and union councils.
History In 1947, when Pakistan gained independence there were 124 districts.
In 1969, 2 new districts (Tangail and Patuakhali) in East Pakistan were formed, bringing the total to 126.
With the Independence of Bangladesh, Pakistan lost 20 of its districts and so there were 106 districts.
In 2001, the number was reduced to 102 by the merger of the 5 districts of Karachi Central, Karachi East, Karachi South, Karachi West and Malir to form Karachi District.

The number of districts rose to 106 again in December 2004, when four new districts were created in the province of Sindh of which one (Umerkot) had existed until 2000 and three districts (Kashmore, Qambar and Jamshoro) were newly created.
The new districts were carved out of Mirpur Khas, Jacobabad, Larkana and Dadu Districts respectively.
In May 2005, the Punjab provincial government created a new district by raising the status of Nankana Sahib from a tehsil of Sheikhupura District to a district in its own right.

On 11 July 2011, the Sindh Government restored again the districts of Karachi South, Karachi East, Malir, Karachi West and Karachi Central, then later in 2013, the district of Korangi was carved out of Karachi East District.
In Azad Jammu and Kashmir, a second-tier of government was formed from three administrative divisions into ten districts.
In Gilgit–Baltistan, there are ten districts divided between the two regions of Gilgit and Baltistan.
In 2018, Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) was merged with Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and FATA agencies were converted into districts.
Chagai is the largest district of Pakistan by area while Lahore District is the largest by population with a total population of 11,126,285 at the 2017 census.
Quetta is the largest district of Balochistan by population with a total population of 2,275,699 at the 2017 census.
Bahawalpur is the largest district of Punjab by area.
Chitral is the largest by area and Peshawar is the largest by population from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with a population of 4,269,079 in the 2017 census.
Sindh's largest district by area is Tharparkar and by population its Karachi West with a population of 3,914,757 in the 2017 census.

The combined population of the six districts of Karachi division is over 16 million in the 2017 census, giving an average population for these six districts of Karachi division of over 2.675 million each.
Neelum and Kotli are the largest districts of Azad Kashmir by area and population respectively.
Gilgit is the largest by area and population both for Gilgit-Baltistan.
As of the 2023 census, all of Pakistan's districts have a muslim majority except for Umerkot district.

District council A district council (or zila council) is a local government body at the district level.

The functions of a district council include construction and maintenance of roads, and bridges, building hospitals and dispensaries, schools and educational institutions, health facilities and sanitation, tube wells for drinking water, rest houses, and coordination of activities of the Union councils within the district.

Fix the water system Pakistan speaks often of agricultural transformation, new seeds, climate-smart technologies, value chains, mechanisation and digital extension.
But every plan rests on a fragile assumption: that water will simply continue to arrive.
The water system on which Pakistan built its agricultural economy is deteriorating faster than any agricultural roadmap can compensate for.
Until that system is rebuilt – governed, measured, regulated and made predictable – agriculture cannot improve.
The Indus Basin Irrigation System feeds more than 90 per cent of Pakistan’s crops, yet a large share of the water released at canal heads never reaches the crop.
Recent empirical work on the Pakistani part of the Indus Basin shows losses of about half across canals, distributaries, watercourses and fields.
Farmers cannot adopt improved seed when water rotations are unpredictable.
A value chain cannot function when tail-end supplies collapse.
In Pakistan, yields do not fall because of farmers’ negligence; they fall because water does not show up.
Groundwater has long served as the country’s silent stabiliser, compensating for unreliable canals.
It now sustains more than half of irrigated agriculture, pumped from about 1.4 million private tubewells.
Peer-reviewed groundwater research shows that lifting 1,000 cubic metres from a shallow tubewell costs about Rs4,225.
For smallholders, this threefold cost difference over the years wipes out profitability.
Case-study modelling in Rechna Doab shows how sensitive agriculture is to depth: when groundwater levels drop from around six metres to over twenty metres, pumping costs rise more than threefold.
The pattern is visible across many canal-command areas, even if depths differ.
Groundwater is becoming too deep and too expensive to sustain the crops it once supported.
Yet Pakistan’s cropping response moves in the opposite direction.
Cotton has been steadily replaced not only by sugarcane and rice, often in the very districts where groundwater tables are falling fastest.
Sugarcane consumes 5,900 to 11,130 cubic metres per acre.
Rice, typically requires 3,240 to 6,070 cubic metres per acre.
Both are dramatically higher than cotton’s requirement of 1,620 to 2,830 cubic metres per acre.
For farmers, sugarcane and rice offer predictable buyers, assured procurement and political backing.
But hydrologically, the shift is self-defeating.
Pakistan is expanding its most water-hungry crops at the exact moment when surface flows are unreliable and groundwater extraction is becoming prohibitively costly.
It locks the country into an impossible equation: declining water availability paired with rising water demand.
The 1991 Water Apportionment Accord provides a binding, rules-based mechanism for allocating flows.
Yet in practice, allocations remain political rather than hydrological.
Telemetry systems, essential for transparency remain contested or non-functional.
Groundwater, despite sustaining most of Pakistan’s agriculture, remains almost entirely unregulated.
The failure of the 2024 IRSA Amendment Ordinance illustrates this paralysis.
The proposal aimed to introduce a national framework for regulating groundwater extraction, aligned with global practice and supported by scientific evidence.
It failed not because the hydrology was disputed but because provinces resisted losing discretionary control.

This leaves Pakistan with a paradox: one of the world’s largest extractors of groundwater, yet with no enforceable safe-yield limits, no aquifer-level accounting and no institutional mechanism linking groundwater use to agricultural planning.
This is a governance failure more than anything else.
Decades of agricultural programming reveal the same lesson.
Even the most advanced interventions fail inside a broken water system.
Drip irrigation delivers marginal gains when canals lose half their supply upstream.
High-yield seed cannot perform when irrigation timings collapse.
Market-linked pulse programmes falter when groundwater depths increase from 10 to 12 metres and pumping costs overwhelm crop returns.
Agricultural programmes often blame ‘farmer adoption constraints’.
In reality, the constraint is water.
Its unreliability, its cost, its politics, and its misgovernance.
If Pakistan wants agriculture to grow, water governance must anchor the agricultural roadmap.
Surface water must move from negotiation-based allocation to real-time, transparent, validated distribution through functional telemetry and enforceable rotational schedules.
Groundwater must be regulated through safe-yield thresholds, licensing of high-capacity tubewells in stressed aquifers, and integration of surface–groundwater planning.
Agricultural incentives must stop rewarding high-delta crops in water-stressed areas and shift toward crops that match hydrological reality.
Farmers cannot be expected to grow water-efficient alternatives when the market, the subsidy regime and the institutional environment push them in the opposite direction.
Where integration between water, agriculture, irrigation and climate departments has occurred, progress is visible.
Where these sectors remain siloed, deterioration accelerates.
The CCI was created precisely to prevent this fragmentation.
It can still fulfil that purpose, if empowered and supported.
Reform disrupts entrenched interests, challenges provincial autonomy narratives, and demands coordination across institutions that have historically avoided collaboration.
But the alternative is certain decline.
Per capita water availability has fallen below scarcity thresholds.
Aquifers in key districts are approaching irreversible depletion.
Climate volatility, from the 2022 floods to the intensified 2025 monsoon, has made agricultural planning dangerously uncertain.
Pakistan does not lack agricultural skill; it lacks water-governance coherence.
Every rupee spent on agricultural development without corresponding investment in water reform is partially wasted.
Every stalled telemetry system, every overridden rotational schedule and every unregulated tubewell pushes agriculture deeper into structural crisis.
If Pakistan wants an agricultural revival, it must begin where agriculture begins, with water.
Fix the water system and agriculture will recover.
Ignore it and no amount of policy, passion or programming will prevent decline.
Water governance is not the parallel track.
The writer is a former Punjab minister for irrigation and finance, with extensive experience in Pakistan’s provincial and federal legislatures.

Oman restores citizenship to 11 people under new royal decree DUBAI: Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq has restored Omani citizenship to 11 people under a royal decree published on Sunday, October 18, in the country’s Official Gazette.
89/2026, issued on October 12, reinstates citizenship for the 11 individuals named in an accompanying list published in Issue No.

The decree’s first article provides for the restoration of nationality to those listed, while its second stipulates that the decree must be published in the Official Gazette and takes effect from the date of its issuance.
The decision was issued after consideration of the Basic Statute of the State and the Omani Citizenship Law introduced under Royal Decree No.
17/2025, and on the grounds of public interest.
What does Oman’s citizenship law say?
Oman’s nationality law, introduced in February 2025, replaced legislation dating from 2014 and sets out the conditions governing the acquisition, loss and restoration of citizenship.
Under Article 7, Omani nationality can be granted, withdrawn, revoked or restored by royal decree following a recommendation from the Minister of Interior.
Article 8 also allows the Sultan to grant or restore citizenship in exceptional circumstances without applying the law’s standard conditions.

The legislation permits Omanis by origin who previously renounced their nationality to acquire another citizenship to apply for its restoration, subject to requirements including residence in Oman or a commitment to return and settle, good conduct and a written declaration of their intention to relinquish their foreign nationality.
The law also provides for the restoration of citizenship to people previously deprived of it when the grounds for its removal no longer apply.
The latest decree does not specify the circumstances under which the 11 individuals previously lost their citizenship or which provisions were applied in their cases.

Adviser to the National Command Authority (NCA) and former director general of the Strategic Plans Division (SPD) retired Lieutenant General Mazhar Jamil has warned of the “risky” outcome for South Asia and beyond of a “dangerous ideology” shaping the Indian military mindset. “Indian military thinking is being shaped by a dangerous ideology, which conflates mythology with national power.

The outcome is very risky and delusional Indian military doctrines with a poor strategic sense of nuclear realities are endangering South Asia and beyond,” he said in his key note address at a workshop titled ‘Nuclear Deterrence and Strategic Stability in South Asia’.
The workshop, held last week in London, was organised by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, which shared a transcript of Jamil’s address late on Monday.
He began by saying that a strategic stability model for a region must take into consideration the political beliefs and strategic thinking of states, which formed the basis of policies.

And that shaped the strategic and security environment in the region, he explained. “The political and strategic thinking of states, therefore, should prefer [a] political approach because military adventurism, hegemonic ambitions are highly risky and unaffordable in the South Asian nuclearised environment,” Jamil stressed, before specifically talking about India and Pakistan.
The two South Asian rivals, he said, had outstanding disputes, Kashmir being the core one. “It needs to be resolved as per the United Nations Security Council resolutions.

But, what we are seeing, on the contrary, is [an] Indian political approach of avoiding the resolution of conflict, because perhaps the Indian leadership believes it has no locus standi on Kashmir when it is presented on the multilateral forums,” Jamil said.
He added that India “tries to manage [the] Kashmir conflict with military violence within occupied Kashmir and through military aggression against Pakistan.
This has not worked, and therefore Kashmir remains a nuclear flashpoint, seriously impacting the South Asian strategic and security environment”.

The security perceptions in South Asia had not evolved in a vacuum, Jamil continued. “Indian revisionist and hegemonic political aspirations have [a] long history of Indian coercion and militant violence against all [of] its neighbours.

Jamil said Bharat was essentially a “revisionist concept that is rooted in reclaiming [the] vast landmass of South Asia and its domination by Hindu civilisation”. “Indian political forces, interestingly, do not shy away anymore in projecting what previous governments pursued covertly.
Very surprisingly, the map of Mahabharat, the greater Bharat, as they call it, covering [the] entire landmass of South Asia, is on the display in the Lok Sabha.

That’s the parliament of India, clearly giving the political direction to the state and the state organisations. “So, no wonder, beyond [the] core nuclear diet of India–Pakistan, India’s conflict with all other countries serves as a perpetual driver of [the] evolving security dynamics in South Asia,” he added.

He also mentioned a recent “political transformation, led by the extremist Hindutva doctrine, that seeks to marginalise and delegitimise [the] non-Hindu population of the state, especially the Muslims”, in India. “This has introduced an additional layer of complexity to the regional security environment.

This marks a significant shift towards a nationalism, which is prejudiced by extreme theological principles,” Jamil said. “So, what we see is that we have a nuclear-armed neighbour whose political and strategic thinking is subordinated to a revisionist, mythological outlook with an overconfidence to subdue its neighbours.

This dangerous political philosophy has trickled into the Indian political, strategic, organisational and even societal culture.” The NCA adviser went on to say that this mindset had also, “unfortunately, penetrated deeply into Indian military thinking”.

He said the first of those lessons was that conflicts outlasted military adventurism and wars, unless they were resolved politically. “The resolution of the Kashmir conflict, therefore, needs a political approach and dialogue to achieve stability at [the] higher political planes,” he asserted.
The second lesson, he said, was that any military misadventurism between two nuclear powers could only escalate the crisis to undesirable consequences and could not serve any purpose to the policy.

In this connection, he added that the Indian leadership needed to understand that it “cannot dictate its unjustified and illegal policy objectives through military aggression to another nuclear power”.
Moving on to the third lesson, Jamil said it was “pivotal to the crisis dynamics of South Asia”.
He then cited military scholar Carl von Clausewitz, who Jamil said had warned that “war is the realm of uncertainty and escalation is really a control ladder”.
Elaborating further, he said: “War is the realm of uncertainty and the lesson from the history of warfare and theory alike is clear.
The Indian strategic approach, he said, sought political and military dominance to be a “regional hegemon with a revisionist political thinking”.
This, however, gave India a false sense of hegemony in the region,” he said.

The second outcome, Jamil said, pertained to the support by Indian technology partners and, “very strangely, also allowing India to get a Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver, in spite of its irresponsible nuclear behaviour”. “Resultantly, India, now, is running one of the fastest-growing nuclear and missile programmes.
This has been done with no regard and concern to arms control, a key factor in the strategic stability for the region.

I think what [we] should now worry about is this ambitious and revisionist state reaching to most of their capitals with no restraints and transparency, even to its own technology partners,” Jamil said.

He said the third outcome was about the policy of appeasement by “certain powers that has made India think that its exceptionalism will always be acceptable to the world”. “Indian propaganda and [its] disinformation campaign was accepted without scrutiny and responsibility.
The case in point is the intentional BrahMos missile attack on Pakistan on 9 March 2022.
Strangely, it took India 48 hours to tell its nuclear neighbour about this incident,” Jamil recalled.
In the 2019 crisis, he pointed out, Modi had bragged at an election rally that India was “not storing nuclear weapons for Diwali”.
India then launched a military offensive despite Islamabad calling for an independent investigation into the incident.

Jamil said that India’s strategy aimed for “escalation domination” and that it planned to intimidate Pakistan via sheer force and the tempo of the operation; however, “Indian planners closely underestimated Pakistan’s resolve and capability”. “The crisis of India’s making could have taken South Asia to the brink of nuclear catastrophe, saved only by the strategic restraint of Pakistan,” he stressed.
He added that Indian leadership had dismissed Pakistan’s nuclear deterrent as “mere nuclear bluff” and boasted about being able to “break Pakistan apart”.
He emphasised that when “rhetorics and confidence” became policy, blunders were likely.

On the other hand, he said, Pakistan’s retaliation was not impulsive but rather had clear political direction and strategic restraint, denying India the space to “normalise coercive conventional aggression”.

He added that Pakistan made the responsible choice not to escalate and to agree to a ceasefire, noting, “I think in all fairness, India owes a thanks to (US) President Trump.” However, he highlighted that this responsible behaviour was being “deliberately misrepresented” by India as a bluff.
Strategic landscape post-2025 Jamil stressed that in the wake of the May 2025 conflict, there was an increased risk of escalation in the region.

He highlighted the “revisionist agenda” of Modi that had “dangerously enhanced the conflict profile” of South Asia by holding the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance, adding to the flashpoint of Kashmir, and continuing with “threats and compellence to another nuclear power”.

He added that India also supported terrorist organisations such as the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), “exporting terrorism as an instrument of policy” to engineer instability in Pakistan. “The space is shrinking between Indian aggressive posturing and Pakistan’s restraint,” he said.

He called on India to shun the policy of supporting terrorist organisations such as the TTP and BLA, noting that Pakistan had presented “irrefutable evidence” of Indian state support to these organisations to the international community and the UNSC.

He also called for the international community to hold India accountable for its involvement in supporting terrorism. “It should be realised that the restraint and strategic patience of Pakistan has its own thresholds,” Jamil stated, adding that “in any future military aggression, the aggressor will have to bear a heavy cost”.
He stressed Pakistan’s readiness to move towards a political dialogue to resolve conflicts, including that of Kashmir, as a responsible nuclear state.

He added that Pakistan offered to establish a robust crisis management mechanism as a first step towards this. “Bharatiya leadership should not be allowed to hold hostage the welfare of two billion people of South Asia, in favour of their hegemonic and delusional revisionist aspirations,” he concluded.

KARACHI: A judicial commission formed to investigate the circumstances and possible negligence in businessman Mir Raza Ali’s murder case has pointed out the police’s “epic failure” in their investigation.
The Sindh cabinet decided to make the report public during a meeting chaired by Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah earlier in the day.

While acknowledging that the initial police response when they were informed of the presence of a body was prompt, the report noted that subsequent events “left a lot to be desired”. “It was a murder,” the report declared.

It explained that the bullet trajectory, the unusual location of the wound if it had been a self-inflicted injury, the “absence of blood, the state of the body, the principles of medical jurisprudence, acid burns and the anaesthesia detected in the blood all clearly excluded suicide as the cause of death”.

The commission determined that releasing the police findings before a proper investigation was “premature and fell short of professional standards”. “Even if the death had been a suicide, the police should have established who was responsible for driving a young man to that point, including whether coercion, blackmail, or instigation was involved.
They made no such effort.” It said the police investigation “failed in its most basic duty: to establish the truth”.

It further observed that “incessant public criticism of the police created problems” as the police “went into a shell, completely broke down communication channels, and took a position based on ego rather than on cogent, solid reasons”.
The report pointed out specific issues with the police conduct: “Lack of leadership, seriousness, and supervision, and, in some cases, negligence by the senior officers.

The handling of this case has been like a rudderless ship, not aware of its destination. “Ranging from negligent to criminally negligent, inexplicable, casual, and unprofessional investigation.” According to the commission, an active cover-up in the initial stages of the investigation cannot be conclusively ruled out.
It noted that senior police officers swept clear investigative lapses under the carpet, without acknowledging them, addressing them, or even attempting to do so. “Too many cooks spoil the broth.

The inquiry said there was a need to mitigate public speculation by an “honest and timely briefing on the investigation”, but this was not done, and the family or the public were not updated through official disclosures. “The police did not follow the commission’s recommendation to appoint a focal person for this reason.
The meeting was attended by Medico-Legal Officer (MLO) Dr Osama Sheikh, who conducted Ali’s first autopsy, the Karachi police chief and other senior officials.

Observations on officials Listing its observations for certain police officials involved in the case, the judicial panel identified “criminal negligence” on the part of Station House Officer (SHO) Adeel Afzal of Ferozabad police station. “Initiate a comprehensive inquiry into him, leading to dismissal from service.
He should be suspended in the interim.
He must also be questioned to determine whether he has facilitated the destruction of key evidence,” the report read.
It also found criminal negligence by Sub-inspector Shabbir Leghari, the first investigating officer (IO) in the case, and called for disciplinary proceedings against him and his suspension.
The report also determined criminal negligence of Inspector Ghaus, but did not recommend any action against him.
Regarding DIG Farukh Lanjar and Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Samiullah Soomro, the commission noted a “lack of leadership and supervision”.

The judicial panel also called out “extreme immaturity” and “childish behaviour” of MLO Sheikh, who conducted the first medico-legal examination, whose findings were later proven incorrect after a second autopsy. “Overconfidence.
Unprofessional conduct not befitting a medical professional.

Must not be assigned medico-legal duties unless he has undergone at least two years of rigorous academic and practical training.” The report said he was “possibly influenced” and called for the angle to be “conclusively determined”.
Suicide vs murder The report also said a voice note provided by Alishaz Mushtaq to police was “one of the most suspicious parts of this case”.
It said that Mushtaq and ASP Nida Junaid, “played a very important role in supporting the police narrative that the death was due to suicide”.
It said that the person Mushtaq named as his source did not corroborate the information he provided, raising suspicion regarding his conduct.

It further said that the WhatsApp messages Ali sent to Sarim Bin Tahir asking for Rs30m, which was “full of uncharacteristic grammatical errors and truncated spellings and read as acute panic”, suggested the deceased was being “blackmailed or threatened”.

It also noted that while CCTV footage showed Ali with a pistol on the night he was killed, this was “unusual”. “All his close friends and associates told the Commission that Raza did not possess or use pistols.
They said he would probably not even know how to handle one.
Witnesses also vouched for his peace-loving, calm, and gentle demeanour.
Why he took the pistol remained a mystery.
The pistol, however, has not been found to date,” it said.
It further said: “The known financial distress was also not of such a nature that would lead a person to suicide.

Ali’s behaviour, until the ride-hailing service dropped him off, did not suggest he was ready to take an extreme step for this reason.” Recommendations Suggesting the next steps, the judicial commission said accommodating the family’s request for a joint investigation team (JIT) was the “most viable path to mitigate ongoing reputational damage to the Government of Sindh”.

It recommended that a JIT be constituted under the leadership of Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Irfan Baloch to “balance the need for public accountability with preserving Sindh Police morale and reputation”.

The report said the team should “integrate senior representatives from the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Intelligence Bureau (IB), Pakistan Rangers (Sindh), and the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) to ensure an impartial, comprehensive, and credible resolution. “This extreme step is necessary to restore public trust and end speculation,” it stressed.

The commission contended that any subsequent police actions will inevitably face heavy public speculation, determining that the police department “bears responsibility for this profound trust deficit between itself and society”. “Even an accurate conclusion or the apprehension of the true culprit is unlikely to be accepted by the public,” it added.
The report pointed out that the case could now “only be resolved through a rigorous, intelligence-based investigation as a “significant portion of physical evidence has been compromised”.

It called for the police to “transparently acknowledge and apologise for past operational lapses”, as well as immediately initiate formal inquiries against the responsible officers in light of the report.

While stating that it did not have investigative powers and that it was difficult to conclude conclusively that an active cover-up occurred, the commission noted that “certain inexplicable actions are difficult to justify and raise the possibility that one may have occurred”.

Therefore, it suggested that a high-level committee, preferably led by the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), be constituted to initiate criminal action against any police officials it finds culpable.
The judicial commission also called for initiating police reforms, particularly to address and modernise the investigation protocol.

It suggested forming a committee of “seasoned professionals” to “specifically address first response, crime scene handling, medico-legal dynamics, collection, safekeeping, and analysis of evidence, and recording the entirety of the investigation in written or digital form”.
While it proposed a three-month timeframe for the exercise, the commission said the Sindh government will make the final decision.
Another suggestion was to consider an increase in the investigation budget, with a protocol in place to monitor the fund’s use.
The panel further suggested steps regarding training of investigators and enhancing the capacity of Crime Scene Units.

Panel formed to ensure implementation The judicial panel’s primary mandate was to determine the facts and circumstances of the case; assess whether police and medico-legal investigations were impartial; identify professional negligence, misconduct, evidence manipulation, or cover-ups; review digital/forensic evidence; and recommend further investigation, forensic analysis, or legal/departmental action.
According to a handout issued by the Sindh chief minister’s spokesperson, the judicial inquiry report was presented in seven separate sealed envelopes.
It will be uploaded on the website of the provincial home department on Tuesday, while a copy will also be provided to the aggrieved family.
Further, CM Shah also constituted a four-member sub-committee to ensure the implementation of the report.
The committee comprises Home Minister Ziaul Hassan Lanjar, Local Government Minister Nasir Hussain Shah, Labour Minister Saeed Ghani and the Sindh advocate general.

Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon also took to X to announce that the report would be made public on Tuesday. “The government of Sindh remains committed to transparency, accountability and ensuring that due process of law is upheld,” he said.

After receiving the record, Abro told reporters that he would hand over the sealed report along with other records to the provincial government and it was the prerogative of the government to decide whether the inquiry report was to be brought into the public domain or otherwise.

In August, the provincial government formed the commission, which was tasked with making recommendations for further investigation and forensic analysis or legal/departmental action, and it was required to submit its findings and recommendations to the Sindh government within 30 days.
However, the commission had struggled to meet its deadline and sent an application last month to the Sindh government for an extension in its tenure till Oct 15.

Amnesty International condemned the severe crackdown on peaceful protesters.

The next day, security forces killed at least three protesters and injured dozens more in Gwadar and Talar.
On July 29, police used tear gas to disperse crowds and detained organizers, including Sammi Baloch, Sibghatullah Shah, and Dr.

Human rights groups including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan condemned the violent crackdowns and called for the release of detained protesters.

• Industrial, services sector slowdown drags down economic growth in FY26 • Per capita income ‘lowest in region’; economy reaches $450.4bn ISLAMABAD: The government on Monday revised the gross domestic product (GDP) growth slightly downward to 3.65 per cent for the outgoing fiscal year (FY26), attributing the adjustment to a mild slowdown in the industrial and services sectors.

The country’s GDP registered modest growth alongside an increase in per capita income in dollar terms, reflecting a sluggish pace of recovery in the country’s overall output compared with the previous year, the government said.
In May 2026, the government had projected the economy to grow by 3.70pc in FY26, revising its earlier estimate of 4pc.
The downward adjustment now indicates that the country fell short of its GDP target.
The revised growth rates in agriculture, industry and services in FY26 are 3.50pc, 3.34pc and 3.81pc, respectively, compared with earlier growth rates of 2.89pc, 3.51pc and 4.09pc.
The revision came during the 118th meeting of the National Accounts Committee (NAC), which was held on Monday at the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics.
The NAC estimate places Pakistan broadly in line with the outlook of multilateral lenders, though with some variation.

The International Monetary Fund has projected GDP growth at 3.6pc for FY26, the World Bank at 3.7pc and the Asian Development Bank at 3.7pc, while the State Bank of Pakistan expects growth to remain close to 3.7pc.

The committee approved the incorporation of revised imports data in the national accounts estimates from FY21 to FY25, quarterly GDP growth rates for Q1 (revised), Q2 (revised), Q3 (revised), and Q4 during FY26 and updated annual growth rates for FY25 and FY26.
The size of the economy rose to $450.4 billion in FY26 from $410.96bn in FY25, mainly driven by growth in the services sector, followed by industry and livestock.
Per capita income slightly increased to $1,896 in FY26, the lowest in the region, up from $1,824 in FY25.
The projection is based on the 2023 census.
However, it was $1,551 in FY23, $1,766 in FY22 and $1,677 in FY21.

This suggests a deterioration in the standard of living and well-being across almost all segments of society, with no tangible increase in personal incomes due to unprecedented inflationary pressures, which reduce disposable income and limit individuals’ ability to afford goods and services, save, or invest.

Updated growth rates Meanwhile, the NAC also approved the updated growth rates for Q1, Q2 and Q3 of 2025-26 at 3.89pc, 4.31pc and 4.42pc, respectively, compared with 3.92pc, 4.05pc and 3.99pc, presented at the 117th meeting of the NAC.
The fourth quarter of FY26 recorded a 2pc growth in GDP.
The committee approved the updated annual growth of 3.11pc for FY25, which was estimated at 3.18pc in the previous meeting.

In agriculture, important crops improved from 0.65pc to 1.59pc due to wheat and maize, other crops have witnessed significant improvement from 2.43pc to 4.28pc due to higher production of pulses (6.3pc), fruits (1.3pc), tomato (44pc), oilseed (5.4pc), and green fodder (2.4pc).
Livestock decreased slightly from 3.75pc to 3.71pc because of increased fodder inputs.
Updated growth rates in forestry and fishing are 10.80pc and 1.39pc, respectively.
The committee revised growth in industry during FY26 to 3.34pc from 3.51pc estimated previously.
The mining & quarrying industry has improved from 0.38pc to 1.52pc due to improvement in gas (2.84pc), crude oil (5.12pc), and coal (2.73pc).
Large-scale manufacturing (LSM), which is measured through the Quantum Index of Manufacturing (QIM), has declined from 6.11pc to 5.01pc.

The major LSM groups with positive contributions are food (7.03pc), tobacco (12.61pc), petroleum products (9.7pc), rubber products (14.19pc), electrical equipment (14.25pc), automobiles (57.77pc), transport equipment (42.36pc), furniture (22.69pc), and other manufacturing (football) (16.62pc).
The construction industry has improved from 5.73pc to 6.30pc because of increased construction-related expenditure in the public sector.
However, some LSM groups posted negative growth, e.g., pharmaceuticals (-8.87pc), iron & steel products (-7.84pc), chemicals (-2.53pc), and leather products (-1.95pc), electricity (-10.24pc) in FY26.
The services industry has declined from 4.09pc to 3.81pc in FY26, with positive contributions from all the constituents.
The growth in wholesale and retail trade posted at 2.37pc as against the previous growth of 3.71pc due to decrease in manufacturing and imports.
Transport and storage industry growth improved to 3.23pc from 2.31pc due to upward revisions reported in railways, water transport, and air transport.
Similarly, information & communication growth increased from 7.52pc to 9.53pc, the finance & insurance also improved from 0.32pc to 4.23pc in FY26 due to improvement in the insurance industry.

Pragmatism over polarity When Pakistan’s first shipment of rare earth minerals quietly departed for the US in October, it drew immediate attention across Asian commentary circles.
Some in China saw betrayal, others in Washington viewed it as an opportunity.

However, in reality, Pakistan’s decision to export rare earths and receive its first crude oil shipment from Houston around the same time signals something more pragmatic than ideological: a bid to regain economic relevance through strategic balance.
Rare earth minerals sit at the heart of today’s technology race.
They power everything from electric vehicles to precision-guided missiles, making them a symbol of strategic dependence.
For years, China has dominated this supply chain, controlling nearly 70 per cent of global production.
Against that backdrop, any new entrant supplying the US naturally raises geopolitical eyebrows.
But Pakistan’s export should not be read as a pivot away from China.
Instead, it reflects Islamabad’s growing recognition that surviving in the current world order requires diversification.
China remains Pakistan’s largest investor and infrastructure partner through the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).
Yet the economic stagnation of recent years, combined with the IMF’s tight fiscal conditions, has forced Islamabad to broaden its options.
Selling minerals to the US and importing energy from Houston are acts of necessity.
For decades, Pakistan’s economic narrative has been shaped by dependency, first on US military and economic aid, then on Chinese loans and projects.
Both relationships brought short-term relief but long-term vulnerability.
The rare earth shipment, though small in volume, reflects an emerging understanding in Islamabad: that sustainability requires trading with everyone and depending on no one.
Pakistan sits atop untapped reserves of copper, lithium and other critical minerals in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
These assets, however, remain trapped under poor infrastructure and limited investment.
Unlike China, Pakistan lacks the capital, refining technology, and logistics network to process these resources domestically.
Partnering with US companies allows the country to monetise what would otherwise stay underground while avoiding over-reliance on a single partner.
In this sense, Pakistan’s rare earth exports are less a geopolitical signal than a developmental strategy.

By opening trade lanes westward, Pakistan aims to attract the type of high-value investment it has historically lacked, investment that generates jobs, builds infrastructure and earns foreign exchange rather than merely incurring debt.
That same pragmatism explains why a crude oil shipment from Houston docked in Karachi almost simultaneously.
This is an experiment in energy diversification driven by affordability.
The fact that the US has now entered Pakistan’s energy matrix underscores how Islamabad is learning to manoeuvre in a multipolar world where ideology matters less than supply security.
It also aligns with Washington’s broader strategic considerations.
The US is actively seeking to ‘de-risk’ its critical mineral supply chain from Chinese dominance.
Engaging with smaller partners like Pakistan serves both strategic and symbolic purposes: it signals that resource security is no longer confined to alliances but open to pragmatic partnerships.
For the US, importing from Pakistan offers limited volume but valuable diversification.
For Pakistan, it provides recognition and leverage.
Beijing’s discomfort with Pakistan’s move is understandable but perhaps overstated.
China has long viewed Pakistan as its strategic partner and buffer in South Asia, not its exclusive economic client.
In fact, a more economically stable Pakistan benefits China’s regional ambitions, particularly the viability of CPEC.
If US engagement helps stabilise Pakistan’s currency, infrastructure and security, Beijing indirectly gains from it.
Moreover, Pakistan’s rare earth exports to the US are unlikely to threaten China’s global dominance in this sector.
The volumes are small, the refining capacity is minimal and the technology gap is wide.
What Islamabad offers instead is optionality, a signal to both great powers that it can cooperate with each without being consumed by either.
Pakistan’s history is littered with moments where it leaned too far towards one power and paid the price.
In the cold war, US aid flowed when Pakistan was useful and dried up when it wasn’t.
In the post-9/11 era, counter-terrorism partnerships brought dollars but also dependency.
More recently, reliance on Chinese loans exposed fiscal vulnerabilities when projects stalled and debt repayments mounted.
This latest round of trade with the US reflects a course correction.
Islamabad appears to be rediscovering a fundamental principle of foreign policy: balance is power.
By trading across geopolitical divides, Pakistan can reassert agency over its economic future.
The move also speaks to a broader trend in global politics.
As the US and China compete for strategic dominance, middle economies like Pakistan, Vietnam and Indonesia are finding room to manoeuvre.
They can extract value from both sides.
Pakistan’s rare earth shipment to the US will not upend global power dynamics, but it does mark a subtle shift in Islamabad’s approach: from ideological alignment to strategic maturity.
Rather than choosing between Washington and Beijing, Pakistan is learning to pick itself, leveraging its geography, resources and partnerships for its own development.

The next step should be to transform these one-off transactions into a coherent national resource policy, one that encourages transparent investment, ensures environmental safeguards and fosters local refining capacity rather than merely exporting raw materials.
That is how Pakistan can convert this moment from symbolism into substance, and from survival into strength.
The writer is a non-resident fellow at the CISS.
